A collection in 50 books of the writings of the great Roman jurists, made on the orders of Justinian between 530 and 533. A commission led by the lawyer Tribonian read some two thousand books and cut them down to about a twentieth, picking passages and fitting them into one system. It came into force at the end of 533.

Most of the text comes from jurists of the 2nd and 3rd centuries, above all Ulpian, who supplies about a third. The Digest is one part of the Corpus Juris Civilis, alongside the Code of imperial laws and the Institutes, a textbook modelled on the Institutes of Gaius.

It had little use in the Latin west for centuries. In the late 11th century a full copy came to light in Italy, and teachers at Bologna began lecturing on it. That revival of Roman law spread across Europe and still shapes the civil law of most of the world.
